Inside the circle there is a horizontal diameter and multiple slanting longitude-line frameworks. The top is marked “A,” the area near the left horizontal line is marked “P,” and the lower-left outside is clearly marked “180°,” which can be used as a reference for the longitude where the date line is located. Then reason together with the question stem: London is located near the 0° meridian, and at this time London is still Saturday; Beijing, calculated by the central meridian of the East Eighth Zone, about 120°E, is already Sunday. The dates of the two places are different, indicating that the natural date boundary, namely the meridian where local time is 0 o’clock, is located between 0° and 120°E. The longitude range that is on the same Sunday as Beijing should extend eastward from this 0 o’clock meridian to the 180° date line marked in the figure. Because the 0 o’clock meridian is already east of 0°, this range is smaller than the half-Earth longitude range from 0° to 180°, that is, smaller than one half of the total number of longitudes. Expressed in option-style wording, it should be “a small half.”

The longitude range that is on the same Sunday as Beijing should extend eastward from this 0 o’clock meridian to the 180° date line marked in the figure. Because the 0 o’clock meridian is already east of 0°, this range is smaller than the half-Earth longitude range from 0° to 180°, that is, smaller than one half of the total number of longitudes. Expressed in option-style wording, it should be “a small half.”
